about: The giant landslides of the main islands as the record maps them: debris fields as Polygons, the scars on the islands where given, the great blocks as Points. Traced by hand on USGS I-2809 (Eakins et al. 2003) and its interpretive inset, fitted to the sheet’s graticule; precision traced (the field’s edge is visible on the sheet) or sketch (drawn round the sheet’s label and texture). Ages in Ma; runout km (record, or measured on the trace); volume km³. See RESEARCH.md §17.

properties.name: Nuʻuanu
properties.scarNote: The flank between the pali crest and the arcuate embayment in the contours about 15 km off today’s shore, where Sherrod et al. (2007, p. 25) put the landslide’s head. They hold the pali itself mainly the work of streams, cut back from that head; the scar polygon is the flank the slide took and the ground the streams wore down after, not a mapped headwall.

blocks.name: Tuscaloosa Seamount
blocks.note: “about 30 km long, 17 km wide, and at least 2 km tall” (ODP Leg 200 report). The point is the block’s centre on I-2809, where the sheet labels it.

properties.note: Traced on I-2809: the west margin and the blocks off the main sheet (Mercator, fitted to its graticule), the outer limit off its interpretive inset, where the Koʻolau shield and its debris are one colour. The record’s run-out (debris avalanches “up to 230 km”, Moore et al. 1989; “more than 200 km”, ODP) runs onto the Hawaiian Arch; the traced toe is about 220 km from Kāneʻohe. Age: 2.1–1.8 Ma (Herrero-Bervera et al. 2002, as the ODP report gives it); Wikipedia (tertiary) has 1–1.5 Ma. Garcia et al. (2006), unread, found several slides in the turbidites of ODP Hole 1223A. Volume: Satake et al. 3,000 km³ of debris (2,000–3,000 km³ missing from the slope); Sherrod et al. 2–4 thousand km³ removed. Area 23,000 km² (Normark et al. 1993, in the ODP report).

properties.name: Wailau
properties.scarNote: The north half of East Molokaʻi; its north pali is now read as the Wailau headwall or its backstepping (Clague and Moore 2002, in Clague and Sherrod 2014, p. 129). Sketched along the north cliffs from Kalaupapa to Hālawa.
properties.note: Traced on I-2809 where its blocks lie north of Molokaʻi, partly among Nuʻuanu’s. Age bracketed, not dated in what was read: after East Molokaʻi’s shield (about 1.5 Ma) and before Kalaupapa grew at the foot of the cliffs (0.57–0.34 Ma, Sherrod et al. 2007, p. 29); about 1.5 Ma is wanted from Clague and Moore 2002. Debris volume 1,500 km³ (Satake et al. 2002). Run-out measured on the trace.

properties.name: Kaʻena
properties.note: Named on I-2809 north of Kaʻena Ridge; traced by eye. Undated in the record read: drawn within Waiʻanae’s life. Kaʻena Ridge may be a volcano of its own (Clague and Sherrod 2014, p. 107).

properties.name: Waiʻanae
properties.note: About 5,500 km², one of the larger Hawaiian slides, slump-like with a complicated and perhaps prolonged history (Sherrod et al. 2007, p. 22). Before about 3.06 Ma if no alkalic rock is in it (Coombs et al. 2004); the erosion before the Kolekole lavas, about 2.98 Ma, may be one of its events (Presley et al. 1997). Traced on I-2809; the sheet’s edge of the lobe is clear on its south and west.

properties.name: North Kauaʻi
properties.note: Named on I-2809; undated in the record read, drawn within Kauaʻi’s shield.

properties.name: South Kauaʻi
properties.note: Named on I-2809; undated. Sherrod et al. (2007, p. 18) favour a landslide origin for the Līhuʻe basin on Kauaʻi’s east side, which may be the head of a slide on that side rather than this one.

properties.name: Clark 1
properties.note: Traced back to Lānaʻi’s outer slope (Sherrod et al. 2007, fig. 17, outlined from Moore et al. 1989); the faults that nearly bisect the island may mark its upper limit. Undated: drawn at the close of Lānaʻi’s shield. I-2809 names two lobes, Clark 1 and Clark 2.

properties.name: Clark 2
properties.note: The distal lobe I-2809 names Clark 2 Slide, south-west of Clark 1; traced by eye.

properties.name: Hāna
properties.note: A sediment-blanketed slump with ridges parallel to old coastlines (I-2809 text). Sketched round the sheet’s label only; undated.

properties.name: Pololū
properties.scarNote: The 20 km indentation of the north-east coast from Waipiʻo to Pololū (Sherrod et al. 2007, p. 41), which they take for the headscarp; Moore et al. (1989) put the head at the summit graben.
properties.note: Late in Pololū time (Pololū lavas 0.45–0.32 Ma; Hāwī lavas, after it, from 0.26 Ma); traced on I-2809 (from Smith et al. 2002 in Sherrod’s fig. 28).

properties.name: Laupāhoehoe
properties.note: Named on I-2809 off the Hāmākua coast; undated.

properties.name: ʻĀlika 2
properties.scarNote: Mauna Loa’s west flank between the Kealakekua and Kahuku faults, where the headwalls of its slides coalesce, the trace between them masked by later lava (Sherrod et al. 2007, p. 50). Sketched; shared with ʻĀlika 1.
properties.note: Emplaced about 125 ka (McMurtry et al. 1999, as Sherrod et al. 2007 give it, p. 7). Two lobes from the same source, as much as 100 km into the Hawaiian Deep, 200–600 km³ together (the value is the middle); the whole slide and slump terrane 1,500–2,000 km³ (Lipman et al. 1988). Traced on I-2809 (Lipman et al. 1988 in Sherrod’s fig. 28).

properties.name: ʻĀlika 1
properties.note: The southern lobe; the two “probably formed in rapid succession”, before a 13 ka reef and after the Nīnole Basalt (Lipman et al. 1988). Its scar is ʻĀlika 2’s.

properties.name: North Kona
properties.note: Named on I-2809; part of the slump terrane west of Mauna Loa and Hualālai that Lipman et al. map. Undated.

properties.name: South Kona
properties.note: Named on I-2809 seaward of the South Kona slump; undated.

properties.name: South Kona slump
properties.note: Named on I-2809. An ancestral slump that cut the shoreline seaward of the Nīnole Hills is thought to have set off their deep erosion (Lipman et al. 1990, in Sherrod et al. 2007, p. 50). Undated.

properties.name: Hilina
properties.note: Kīlauea’s south flank moving now: slumps may creep or surge forward several metres, causing the largest of Hawaiʻi’s historic earthquakes, in 1868 and 1975 (Moore et al. 1994). Drawn at the present; the age is “now”, not a date. Traced on I-2809.
